query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the number of principal elements from the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni configuration to quaternary or ternary compositions decreases the extent of nanocluster formation at grain boundaries and dampens local chemical fluctuations near stacking faults, resulting in enhanced grain boundary cohesion and more uniform stacking fault energies that delay crack initiation and yield more uniform ductile deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy processed to form a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Prepare alloys by systematically removing one or more elements to form quaternary or ternary versions while replicating identical thermomechanical processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Under controlled thermomechanical processing and intermediate-temperature tensile testing conditions where GB decohesion is critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical segregation (nanoclustering) at grain boundaries and the degree of local compositional fluctuations affecting stacking fault energetics.
generation.mechanism: A reduced number of elements limits the chemical driving force for separate nanoclusters (e.g., of Cr, Ni, and Mn) at GBs and moderates fluctuations in local stacking fault energies. This dual effect increases GB cohesion and promotes a more homogeneous deformation mechanism (e.g., reduced premature crack initiation and steadier strain hardening).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic quinary HEA baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will display lower incidences of GB nanoclustering (as measured by atom probe tomography), smaller variations in stacking fault energy, delayed onset of GB cracking, and improved uniform ductility during tensile deformation.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy under identical processing and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply within single-phase FCC HEA or MEA systems under similar thermomechanical and testing regimes, particularly where intermediate-temperature deformation governs ductility via grain boundary behavior.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain to what extent the reduction in local chemical fluctuations and nanoclustering individually versus synergistically improves mechanical performance, and whether other microstructural factors might also dominate under different processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of equiatomic (quinary), quaternary, and ternary alloys with similar single-phase FCC microstructures via identical thermomechanical processing. Characterize the alloys using atom probe tomography to quantify nanocluster distribution at grain boundaries, and measure local stacking fault energy distributions through first-principles calculations or local probe techniques. Perform intermediate-temperature tensile tests to assess ductility, strain-hardening rates, and onset of GB cracking.
measurements: Quantification of nanocluster size and density at grain boundaries
Distribution of local stacking fault energies
Tensile ductility (failure strain) and strain-hardening behavior
Onset temperature and incidence of GB cracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If quaternary and ternary alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in GB nanoclustering and local SFE variability or if they do not show improved ductility and delayed GB cracking compared to the equiatomic quinary baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

## Abstract
Medium and high entropy alloys (MEAs and HEAs) based on 3d transition metals, such as face-centered cubic (fcc) CrCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi alloys, reveal remarkable mechanical properties. The stacking fault energy (SFE) is one of the key ingredients that controls the underlying deformation mechanism and hence the mechanical performance of materials. Previous experiments and simulations have therefore been devoted to determining the SFEs of various MEAs and HEAs. The impact of local chemical environment in the vicinity of the stacking faults is, however, still not fully understood. In this work, we investigate the impact of the compositional fluctuations in the vicinity of stacking faults for two prototype fcc MEAs and HEAs, namely CrCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi by employing first-principles calculations. Depending on the chemical composition close to the stacking fault, the intrinsic SFEs vary in the range of more than 150 mJ/m2 for both the alloys, which indicates the presence of a strong driving force to promote particular types of chemical segregations towards the intrinsic stacking faults in MEAs and HEAs.
